newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian buyers await U.S. soybean/corn crop data.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian buyers await U.S. soybean/corn crop data.

text.p: Southeast Asian grain and oilseeds buyers are standing on the sidelines waiting for a clearer picture of the U.S. soybean and corn crop before deciding to buy, regional traders said on Thursday.
"The buyers are standing aside. The $64,000 question is when they're all going to jump in," a trader with a U.S. commodity house said.

"If I don't do any business soon, I'm going to start killing people," a Western commodity house trader said before breaking out into a laugh. "The buyers here are all waiting for the prices to come down some more."

A combination of ideal harvest weather and reports of better-than-expected yields in the U.S. along with rumours China may export anything between 1.0-4.0 million tonnes of corn early in 1997 weighed on the market and may drive prices lower, traders said.

December corn on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) closed on Wednesday 3-1/4 U.S. cents lower at $2.92-3/4 a bushel after fears of a killing frost waned, traders said. CBOT corn has shed about 45 cents a bushel in the last three weeks.
The November CBOT soybean contract slid 7-1/4 U.S. cents to end on Wednesday at $7.42 a bushel.
Prices will probably remain soft after U.S.-based analysts said any damage from a cold front sweeping into the U.S. Midwest may be light.
U.S. corn in Southeast Asia is being quoted at around $156-$160 a tonne C&F on a Panamax vessel for November-December shipment, dealers said.

"Regional demand looks a little bit weak. People are really holding back to wait for the U.S. harvest. Many of the people are also well-covered to the year-end," one said. "There's some business being done, but we've seen nothing big so far."
On Chinese corn export licences, one trader said: "It's not yet a factor, but it's looming over the market."
"Our guess about Chinese corn exports is one to two million tonnes. Some people say it might reach three to four million tonnes," a grains analyst said.

Talk was also circulating in the market that some Indonesian buyers washed out contracts for up to 70,000 tonnes of corn in the hope of buying Chinese corn, one trader said. Others said the washout was more likely to be due to the expectation of lower U.S. prices later in the year and a good local harvest.
The only business being done in the region is for soymeal, where demand remained strong.

Indonesia is making inquiries for 100,000 tonnes of soymeal while Malaysia, which recently clinched a deal for 25,000 tonnes of South American meal, is seeking about 75,000 tonnes, a dealer in a European commodity house said.
"Indonesia may buy three or four cargoes of soymeal reaching 100,000 tonnes, but there's no word from them right now," the trader said.
But other traders said both countries may just sit it out for now to wait for U.S. soymeal to come into the market, which is currently quoted slightly lower than Indian meal.

U.S. meal is being quoted at around $307-$309 a tonne C&F Southeast Asia on board a Panamax vessel for November/December shipment while Indian meal is priced at $316-$318 a tonne C&F for the same shipment period, dealers said.
Some buyers are also looking at soymeal from Brazil or Argentina, but would want a look at the new U.S. crop before making any decision, traders said.
"Demand for corn, beans and meal in the region is still there. The only question facing buyers right now is the timing of their purchases," one trader said.
- Singapore newsroom (65-8703305)
